subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Indian Tea Plantations
description: A fast breakdown of Indian Tea Plantations for builders.

hook.text: Wild tea plants grew in India's Assam region for centuries. The British didn't notice until 1823.

buildup.text: Major Robert Bruce found native Assam tea plants. The British realized they didn't need China at all.

discovery.text: By 1860, massive plantations covered Assam and Darjeeling. India became the world's largest tea producer.

twist.text: Plantation labor was brutal. Workers were indentured, paid almost nothing, and couldn't leave.

climax.text: India still produces over 1.3 billion kg of tea annually—second only to China in global output.

punchline.text: Britain wanted independence from China's tea. India paid the price.

quiz.question: Where were wild tea plants discovered in India?

details.summary: The British established vast tea plantations in Assam and Darjeeling starting in the 1830s. They used exploitative labor systems, including indentured workers from other regions.
details.whyItMatters: Indian plantations made tea a global commodity but at enormous human cost. The labor structures established then continue to shape workers' conditions today.
takeaways: British plantations in Assam and Darjeeling started in the 1830s
Exploitative labor systems including indentured workers were used
India became the world's largest tea producer by the 1900s

faq.question: What were labor conditions like on colonial tea plantations?
faq.answer: Conditions were brutal. Workers, often brought from distant regions under misleading contracts, faced long hours, low pay, poor housing, and harsh discipline. Malaria and other diseases were rampant. The power imbalance between British planters and Indian workers was extreme and systemic.

faq.question: Have conditions improved on Indian tea plantations today?
faq.answer: Progress has been uneven. Workers' rights and wages have improved through unionization and regulation, but many plantation workers still earn very low wages and live in outdated housing. Certification programs try to raise standards, but systemic issues remain in parts of the industry.
